sections.theory:
Measurement of economic development (Measurement of Economic Development)

Before economists this has been the problem: for measuring economic development which touchstone be used, or which change be considered the indication (Indication) from which it becomes known whether economic development has occurred or not, and if it has occurred, how much? Among experts there is considerable difference about this indication, as appears from their opinions. Different experts consider the following as the indication of economic development:

1. Increase in national production

By economic development is meant increase in national income or national production.

2. Increase in per capita income

By economic development is meant increase in per capita income.

3. Increase in production per labourer

The indication of economic development is that production per labourer increases.

4. Increase in the importance of secondary occupations

The manifestation of progress is that the importance of primary means of employment, e.g. agriculture, mining and fishing etc., becomes less, and instead of them the importance of occupations of a secondary nature, e.g. industry, construction, communications and trade, increases.

5. Increase in the production of capital goods (Capital Goods)

The indication of economic development is that, compared with the production of consumer goods, an increase goes on occurring in the production of capital goods, e.g. machines etc.

6. Increase in the rate of investment

Economic development is expressed by this, that the speed of investment (Investment) increases from before.

Methods of measuring economic development

1. Increase in real national income

The supporters of this method are Meier, Baldwin, Snider and Kindleberger. According to these experts, if continuous increase is occurring in the real national income of a country, then that country is moving on the path of progress. In contrast, if the real national income of that country is not increasing, then that country is not progressing. These experts have made real national income, instead of money income, the standard of progress, i.e. that income will be kept in view after removing the effect of prices. In this connection the rate of progress should not be ignored. Therefore it is necessary to keep in view both the standard of national income and the rate of increase in it. A country which is progressing at a higher rate can soon get ahead of a country with more income than itself.

Obstacles

In this method the following obstacles stand in the way:

(i) Correct statistics not being available.

(ii) Because of taxes and subsidies, the correct price of things not being estimated.

(iii) Non-cooperation of the public.

Measurement of economic development (Measurement of Economic Development)

Before economists this has been the problem: for measuring economic development which touchstone be used, or which change be considered the indication (Indication) from which it becomes known whether economic development has occurred or not, and if it has occurred, how much? Among experts there is considerable difference about this indication, as appears from their opinions. Different experts consider the following as the indication of economic development:

1. Increase in national production

By economic development is meant increase in national income or national production.

2. Increase in per capita income

By economic development is meant increase in per capita income.

3. Increase in production per labourer

The indication of economic development is that production per labourer increases.

4. Increase in the importance of secondary occupations

The manifestation of progress is that the importance of primary means of employment, e.g. agriculture, mining and fishing etc., becomes less, and instead of them the importance of occupations of a secondary nature, e.g. industry, construction, communications and trade, increases.

5. Increase in the production of capital goods (Capital Goods)

The indication of economic development is that, compared with the production of consumer goods, an increase goes on occurring in the production of capital goods, e.g. machines etc.

6. Increase in the rate of investment

Economic development is expressed by this, that the speed of investment (Investment) increases from before.

Methods of measuring economic development

1. Increase in real national income

The supporters of this method are Meier, Baldwin, Snider and Kindleberger. According to these experts, if continuous increase is occurring in the real national income of a country, then that country is moving on the path of progress. In contrast, if the real national income of that country is not increasing, then that country is not progressing. These experts have made real national income, instead of money income, the standard of progress, i.e. that income will be kept in view after removing the effect of prices. In this connection the rate of progress should not be ignored. Therefore it is necessary to keep in view both the standard of national income and the rate of increase in it. A country which is progressing at a higher rate can soon get ahead of a country with more income than itself.

Obstacles

In this method the following obstacles stand in the way:

(i) Correct statistics not being available.

(ii) Because of taxes and subsidies, the correct price of things not being estimated.

(iii) Non-cooperation of the public.

2. Increase in per capita income

The supporters of this method are Professor Arthur Lewis, Jacob Viner, H. F. Williamson and Leibenstein. According to them a country progresses at that time when its per capita income is increasing. Per capita income is obtained by dividing national income by population. Per capita income can increase only in that case when the rate of increase in income is more and the rate of increase in population is less.

Obstacles

In this method the following obstacles stand in the way:

(i) Correct statistics not being available.

(ii) Per capita income alone is not a guarantee of the standard of living.

(iii) Per capita income shows the distribution of income as always equal, which is not possible in practical life.

(iv) In the opinion of most experts, per capita income is not the best method of measuring economic development.

3. Standard of living as a measure of economic development

Modern experts are not satisfied with both the above methods. Among these experts Norman Hicks and Paul Streeten are included. According to them a country progresses at that time when the basic necessities of life are available to it in a better way. In these basic necessities the following are included:

(i) facilities of health; (ii) better education; (iii) good food and housing; (iv) water supply and drainage; (v) means of transport.

Because of these facilities basic needs will be satisfied and poverty will decrease.

Problems of developing economy (Problems of Developing Economy)

Less developed or developing (Developing) countries and economies face the following problems. Pakistan too is a developing country, because in it the following characteristics are found:

1. Low per capita income (Low Per.capita Income)

In semi-developed countries per capita income is very little, whereas in developed countries it is more; e.g. at this time in Japan the average annual per capita income is 33 thousand dollars, and in the United States of America more than thirty-five thousand dollars. Therefore the residents of semi-developed countries cannot fulfil even the basic necessities of their daily life well.

2. Over-population (Population Pressures)

One problem of semi-developed countries is that their population is more than their resources, and the speed of population growth too is fast. In the opinion of experts their resources cannot bear the growing population; therefore the standard of living has settled at a low level.

2. Increase in per capita income

The supporters of this method are Professor Arthur Lewis, Jacob Viner, H. F. Williamson and Leibenstein. According to them a country progresses at that time when its per capita income is increasing. Per capita income is obtained by dividing national income by population. Per capita income can increase only in that case when the rate of increase in income is more and the rate of increase in population is less.

Obstacles

In this method the following obstacles stand in the way:

(i) Correct statistics not being available.

(ii) Per capita income alone is not a guarantee of the standard of living.

(iii) Per capita income shows the distribution of income as always equal, which is not possible in practical life.

(iv) In the opinion of most experts, per capita income is not the best method of measuring economic development.

3. Standard of living as a measure of economic development

Modern experts are not satisfied with both the above methods. Among these experts Norman Hicks and Paul Streeten are included. According to them a country progresses at that time when the basic necessities of life are available to it in a better way. In these basic necessities the following are included:

(i) facilities of health; (ii) better education; (iii) good food and housing; (iv) water supply and drainage; (v) means of transport.

Because of these facilities basic needs will be satisfied and poverty will decrease.

Problems of developing economy (Problems of Developing Economy)

Less developed or developing (Developing) countries and economies face the following problems. Pakistan too is a developing country, because in it the following characteristics are found:

1. Low per capita income (Low Per.capita Income)

In semi-developed countries per capita income is very little, whereas in developed countries it is more; e.g. at this time in Japan the average annual per capita income is 33 thousand dollars, and in the United States of America more than thirty-five thousand dollars. Therefore the residents of semi-developed countries cannot fulfil even the basic necessities of their daily life well.

2. Over-population (Population Pressures)

One problem of semi-developed countries is that their population is more than their resources, and the speed of population growth too is fast. In the opinion of experts their resources cannot bear the growing population; therefore the standard of living has settled at a low level.
